subject: AIC/BIC versus CV small data sets - Error: argument 1 (type 'list') cannot be handled by 'cat'

messages.author: b0eaaa355885abf4
messages.subject: AIC/BIC versus CV small data sets - Error: argument 1 (type 'list') cannot be handled by 'cat'
parts:
Hi Chris,

I am trying to run an occurrence distribution for one dataset of one hawk for which I have Argos telemetry data. Everything up to model selection worked fine, but then I was trying to get the plot I got the following error message "Error: argument 1 (type 'list') cannot be handled by 'cat".

After discussing this briefly with you, you suggested me to use the LOOCV as the model selection criteria instead of the default AIC/BIC given that my sample size is small (small dataset for the birds and coarsely sampled).

Could you guide me on how to do this? Where should I change/choose the LOOCV over the AIC/BIC? And also, how to determine when is best to use the AIC/BIC and when the LOOCV?

Many thanks

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: AIC/BIC versus LOOCV/HSCV - Re: Error: argument 1 (type 'list') cannot be handled by 'cat'
parts:
Hi Sandra,

Important properties of AIC/BIC:
  1. Asymptotically (with lots of data), and given a true model, AIC is equivalent to fitting the model to a training dataset, and then cross validating with an independent validation dataset via likelihood.
  2. Asymptotically, AIC essentially provides a point estimate for the KL divergence (a measure of dissimilarity) between the true model and the fitted model. So, minimizing AIC is (asymptotically) minimizing dissimilarity with the truth.
  3. Asymptotically, and with linear models, AIC gives optimal predictions but is not asymptotically consistent (does not necessarily converge on the true model if there are many candidate models). In contrast, and under the same conditions, BIC is asymptotically consistent, but does not give optimal predictions. [It is impossible for one IC to have both asymptotically optimal predictions and asymptotic consistency.]
AICc is a slight upgrade to AIC (2) for small sample sizes, in that AICc provides an unbiased point estimate of the KL divergence, under the assumption that the fitted model is the true model. [Furthermore, the AICc value in ctmm is approximate, except for IID models, where it is exact. You can calculate AICc more exactly via simulation, but I have not found this very worthwhile so far.]

AIC/BIC, and even AICc, don't have very good properties for small amounts of data, to my knowledge, and in my experience. With small amounts of data, I have implemented two cross-validated-likelihood information criteria---"LOOCV" and "HSCV" (https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/ctmm.fit.html), which are mathematically analogous to AIC (1), but do not assume a true model. In each case, part of the data is used as training data, to fit the model to, and the other part of the data is used as validation data, to see how well the fitted model performs out-of-sample. Because the data are autocorrelated, there is no one best way to split the data into training and validation data. Therefore, the way you split the data determines what the selected model will be best suited for.

"LOOCV" leaves out one fix from the training dataset and then validates it. This is done for all fixes, multiplying their out-of-sample probabilities together. "LOOCV" is more suited for fine-scale estimates like calculating occurrence distributions. But, you have to fit a model for every fix, making this method too slow for large datasets.

"HSCV" fits to the first half of the data and validates the second half (and vice versa). "HSCV" is more suited to coarse-scale estimates like calculating home-range distributions.

[Another popular method is block-wise CV, but I'm not aware of a non-arbitrary choice of block sizes, so I have not yet implemented this.]

From the command line, model selection is then performed with the IC argument supplied (the default is the approximate "AICc") like

FITS <- ctmm.select(DATA,GUESS,IC="LOOCV",verbose=TRUE)

The first model will be the selected model, as usual. But if using summary on the candidate models, you also have to use the IC argument, or it will again default to the approximate "AICc".

summary(FITS,IC="LOOCV")

If I had a lot of datasets, where some were too small for AIC and some were too large for LOOCV, then I would check that as the sample size increases the LOOCV-best results become insubstantially different from the AIC-best results. Unless something pathological is happening, I would expect the results to converge, given property (1) of AIC.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: AIC/BIC versus LOOCV/HSCV - Re: Error: argument 1 (type 'list') cannot be handled by 'cat'
parts:
Hi Sandra,

There is no way to choose IC="LOOCV" in ctmmweb at the moment, and ctmmweb isn't going to see the FITS argument from that command. I was just giving an example of how to do this from the command line. You would want to stay on the command line, run occurrence(), and then run the export function that you want. Potentially, you could look at the output of summary(FITS,IC="LOOCV") on the command line and then manually select the LOOCV-best model in ctmmweb, but I don't think that would be easier.

https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/occurrence.html
https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/export.html

Best,
Chris
